name: Mizo
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Laltleipuii. 2018 [deposited 2019]. Interpersonal Function of Tones in Mizo. PhD thesis, Department of Linguistics and Contemporary English, The English and Foreign Languages University, Hyderabad (supervisor C. Meena Debashish). Open copy: archive.org item;gov.tribals.74190 (= Shodhganga 10603/347993).
catalog_locator: Ch.1 sec. 1.5.2.1 'Tonic Prominence', pp.24-27 with fn.22 (p.27); tone inventory sec. 1.5.2 p.20 fn.17 and sec. 6.1.1 p.298; restatement sec. 6.1.2 p.299 and p.282. copies we hold re-extracted with; scan copy.
catalog_quote: Unlike English, such shifting of the tonic prominence to indicate emphasis or contrast is not possible in Mizo; the tonic prominence cannot be relocated to certain parts in the clause for indicating a change in information focus. ... One main difference on comparing the examples from both the languages is that while the shift in tonic prominence is possible in English to suit the context, the tonic is always on the last syllable of the tone group in Mizo. ... During analysis, it was observed that the most prominent pitch change was always on the last syllable [fn.22] of the clause. The tonic syllable, i.e. the final syllable in the tone group, exhibited changes in intensity, duration and pitch. It always has a higher pitch or longer duration, or in the case of some attitudes, the tone completely changes or is more prominently pronounced. [fn.22] This is not just in the case of contextualized examples of Chapter 4. Even in the drama (continuous speech) text, we find the tonic prominence always on the last syllable of a tone group (see examples in Chapter 5).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mizo is a four-tone language; the only prominence the source describes is phrasal: the tonic (nuclear) prominence falls on the final syllable of the tone group/clause and cannot be moved for focus or contrast (emphasis is expressed by added pronouns, adverbs or negation instead). No word-level stress rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: p.298: tonic prominence is never allocated to negation elements, but 'in the case of adverbials, sometimes, the adverbials are selected for tonic prominence'.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone group / clause (Hallidayan intonation unit), established instrumentally (Praat) on contextualised clauses and a continuous drama text; not a statement about the citation-form word. The only work addressing word-level stress directly (Ramdinmawii & Nath 2022, paywalled) reports in its abstract that H-tone syllables of disyllables are 'generally stressed' without a positional rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Laltleipuii 2018 describes standard Mizo (Lusei/Duhlian ṭawng) as spoken in Aizawl-area informants (EFLU study); Chhangte 1989 describes the Southern Duhlian dialect of Lunglei; Lorrain & Savidge 1898 the 'Dulien dialect'. All are lush1249. Soppitt 1887's accent rules belong to Rangkhol/Hrangkhol (hran1239), not Mizo.

sources.note: Hallidayan instrumental (Praat) study of Mizo tone/intonation. Sec. 1.5.2.1 'Tonic Prominence' (p.24-27) and 6.1.2 (p.298): the tonic (most prominent) syllable is always the last syllable of the tone group/clause in Mizo and cannot be relocated for focus/contrast; prominence realised by duration, intensity, pitch. No word-level stress rule; 'stress' used only in the sense of semantic emphasis.

sources.citation: Lalhminghlui, Wendy. 2023. The Phonetics and Phonology of Tones in Mizo. PhD thesis, Dept. of Humanities and Social Sciences, IIT Guwahati (gyan.iitg.ac.in handle 123456789/2685; Shodhganga 10603/472163).
sources.note: Four lexical tones (H, L, rising, falling), TBU = sonorant rhyme, rising-tone sandhi, tone-consonant and tone-vowel interaction. The word 'stress' does not occur in the body text; silent on word stress. Useful literature review naming Henderson 1948, Weidert 1975, Fanai 1992, Chhangte 1993, Lalthangliana 1997.

sources.citation: Lalthangliana. 1997. Aspects of Mizo in the structural paradigm. PhD thesis, Gauhati University.
sources.note: Structuralist description with phonology chapters (five-tone analysis); may contain a stress/juncture section.

sources.citation: Fanai, Lalrindiki T. 1992. Some Aspects of the Lexical Phonology of Mizo and English: An Autosegmental Approach. PhD thesis, CIEFL (EFLU) Hyderabad.
sources.note: The most detailed native-speaker phonology (syllable structure, tone linking, lexical phonology); a lexical-phonology treatment comparing Mizo with English is likely to address stress/metrical structure explicitly.
